title: Quicksort, quickselect, sorting bounds, counting/radix
summary: Quicksort partitions around a pivot and recurses; it is Θ(N log N) expected but Θ(N²) on bad pivots. Quickselect finds the k-th smallest in expected linear time. No comparison sort can beat Θ(N log N) because log₂(N!) comparisons are needed, but counting sort and LSD/MSD radix sorts avoid comparisons entirely. Exams trace partitions and radix passes and ask you to choose a sort under constraints.

blocks.text: Rearrange so that every item left of x is ≤ x and every item right of x is ≥ x. Then x is in its final sorted position; sort both sides recursively.
Simple 3-way partition (lecture demo version): pivot = leftmost item; scan left to right, copying items into three lists — smaller, equal, larger — and concatenate. Stable, but uses Θ(N) extra space.

blocks.title: Quicksort with the 3-way list partition
steps: Pivot 4: smaller [1, 2], equal [4, 4, 4], larger [7, 9, 6] (each list keeps arrival order).
Concatenate: 1 2 4 4 4 6 7 9. Duplicates of the pivot are finished after the first partition.

blocks.text: Partitioned ≠ sorted: after one partition only the pivot (and its duplicates in the 3-way version) is guaranteed to be in final position.

blocks.title: Hoare partition with pivot p = a[lo]
items: L starts at lo + 1 and moves right while a[L] < p (it stops on items ≥ p).
G starts at hi and moves left while a[G] > p (it stops on items ≤ p).
If L < G, swap a[L] and a[G], step both inward, repeat. Otherwise stop.
Swap the pivot a[lo] with a[G]; return G.

blocks.title: Hoare partition trace
steps: L stops at index 1 (9); G stops at index 7 (3): swap → [6 3 2 7 4 1 8 9].
L moves from 2: 2 < 6, stops at index 3 (7); G moves from 6: 8 > 6, stops at index 5 (1): swap → [6 3 2 1 4 7 8 9].
L moves from 4: 4 < 6, stops at index 5 (7); G moves from 4: 4 ≤ 6, stops at index 4. L ≥ G: stop.
Swap pivot with index 4: [4 3 2 1 6 7 8 9]; pivot index 4.

blocks.name: Why stop on equal items
blocks.text: Both pointers stop on items equal to the pivot and swap them, spreading duplicates across both sides. On [4 4 4 4 4 4 4] the pivot lands at index 3 (the middle), so all-equal arrays stay Θ(N log N). A partition that sends all equal items to one side is Θ(N²) on them.

items: Full quicksort of [6 9 2 7 4 1 8 3] then partitions [4 3 2 1] (pivot to index 3), [1 3 2] (pivot 1 stays), [3 2] → [2 3], and [7 8 9] trivially: [1 2 3 4 6 7 8 9] (verified).

blocks.title: Measure the worst case
blocks.prompt: Count comparisons of leftmost-pivot Hoare quicksort on sorted vs random input, N = 1000 and 2000.
steps: Sorted input: every partition peels off only the pivot: (N − 1) + (N − 2) + ⋯ ≈ N²/2. Measured 500,499 and 2,000,999 (×4 when N doubles).
Random input: measured 12,196 and 25,675 (≈ ×2.1 when N doubles): Θ(N log N).

blocks.name: Why expected Θ(N log N)
blocks.text: A random pivot lands in the middle half with probability 1/2, leaving pieces ≤ 3/4 of the size. So along any path the size shrinks by 3/4 every couple of levels: O(log N) depth, Θ(N) partition work per level. Even a consistent 10%/90% split gives depth log_{10/9} N = Θ(log N).

items: Defenses: shuffle first, pick a random pivot, or median-of-three. Choosing the exact median as pivot (via linear-time selection) guarantees Θ(N log N) but is slow in practice.
Quicksort uses Θ(log N) expected stack space; in practice it is the fastest general-purpose comparison sort (Java’s primitive sort is a dual-pivot quicksort).

blocks.text: To find the k-th smallest (0-based index k, e.g. the median), partition once. If the pivot lands at index j = k, done; otherwise continue in only the side containing k.

blocks.title: Quickselect trace
blocks.prompt: Find the item at sorted index 3 (the 4th smallest) of [6, 9, 2, 7, 4, 1, 8, 3] with Hoare partitioning.
steps: Partition all: [4 3 2 1 6 7 8 9], pivot at 4 > 3 → continue in [0..3].
Partition [4 3 2 1] (pivot 4): it lands at index 3 = k: [1 3 2 4 …].

blocks.name: Quickselect runtime
blocks.text: Expected Θ(N): sizes shrink geometrically, N + N/2 + N/4 + ⋯ ≈ 2N on average. Worst case Θ(N²): finding the median of sorted [1 … 9] with a leftmost pivot partitions [0..8], [1..8], [2..8], [3..8], [4..8] before returning 5 (verified) — each partition removes one item.

blocks.name: Ω(N log N) for comparison sorts
blocks.text: A comparison sort must distinguish all N! orderings of the input. Each comparison has two outcomes, so after c comparisons at most 2ᶜ orderings can be told apart: 2ᶜ ≥ N!, i.e. c ≥ log₂(N!) ∈ Θ(N log N).

proof.text: log₂(N!) ≥ log₂((N/2)^(N/2)) = (N/2) log₂(N/2) gives the Ω; log₂(N!) ≤ N log₂ N gives the O.

blocks.title: Minimum worst-case comparisons
blocks.prompt: What is the minimum worst-case number of comparisons to sort 3, 5, 8 and 20 items? Can 20 items be sorted with 61 comparisons?
steps: log₂ 3! = 2.58 → at least 3. log₂ 5! = log₂ 120 = 6.91 → at least 7. log₂ 8! = 15.30 → at least 16.
log₂ 20! = 61.08 → at least 62. So 61 comparisons can never suffice for 20 items.

blocks.text: The bound applies only to comparison sorts and only to the worst case. Insertion sort is Θ(N) on sorted input, and counting/radix sorts beat N log N by not comparing.

blocks.title: Counting sort for keys 0 … R−1
items: Count occurrences of each key: Θ(N).
Turn counts into starting positions (running sums): Θ(R).
Scan the input left to right, placing each item at its key’s next free position: Θ(N). Left-to-right scanning makes it stable.

blocks.title: Counting sort trace
steps: Counts: key0 1, key1 2, key2 1, key3 3.
Starts: key0 0, key1 1, key2 3, key3 4.

blocks.name: Cost
blocks.text: Θ(N + R) time and space. Excellent when R = O(N); hopeless when R is huge (keys up to 2³¹).

LSD radix sort: sort by the last digit, then the second-to-last, …, finally the first, using a stable sort (counting sort) per digit. Stability preserves the order established by less significant digits.

blocks.title: LSD radix trace (base 10)
steps: Ones digit: 720 355 035 436 457 657 329 839 (355 before 035: both 5, input order).

blocks.name: LSD cost
blocks.text: W passes of counting sort: Θ(W(N + R)). For N 32-bit ints with R = 256: 4 passes, Θ(N).

MSD radix sort: sort by the first character into buckets, then recursively sort each bucket by the next character (never re-sort across buckets). Stops early in buckets of size 1, so it can examine far fewer than all characters. Worst case (many equal prefixes) Θ(W(N + R)); per-bucket count arrays make it costly for small buckets.

blocks.title: Why MSD must recurse within buckets
blocks.prompt: Words cab, bee, dab, bad, add, bed, ace, dad. Do the first MSD pass, then show what goes wrong if you instead re-sort the whole array by the second letter.
steps: Pass 1 (stable, by first letter): add ace bee bad bed cab dab dad. Buckets a: {add, ace}, b: {bee, bad, bed}, c: {cab}, d: {dab, dad}.
Correct: sort each bucket by the next letters: ace add | bad bed bee | cab | dab dad.
Wrong: re-sorting everything by the 2nd letter gives bad cab dab dad ace add bee bed — the first-letter order is destroyed.
blocks.answer: ace add bad bed bee cab dab dad (verified)

blocks.text: LSD requires a stable per-digit sort. With an unstable one (e.g. heapsort), LSD on 31, 12, 21, 22 can end as 12 22 21 31 (verified with a tie-reversing per-digit sort). MSD does not rely on stability because each bucket is fully sorted on the remaining characters.

hard.title: Sort N integers in [0, N²) in Θ(N)

prompt.text: You must sort N integers, each in 0 … N² − 1, in Θ(N) time. Comparison sorts and plain counting sort are both too slow — why? Give a linear algorithm and trace it on N = 10: 73, 5, 99, 42, 18, 64, 0, 57, 31, 86.

hard.answer: LSD radix sort with radix N (2 passes); result 0 5 18 31 42 57 64 73 86 99

solution.text: Comparison sorts need Ω(N log N). Counting sort needs R = N² buckets: Θ(N²).
Write each key in base N: two digits (x mod N, then x / N), each in 0 … N − 1. LSD radix sort with counting sort per digit: 2 passes × Θ(N + N) = Θ(N).
Generalization: keys in [0, N^c) take c passes: Θ(cN).

hard.title: Lower-bound puzzles

prompt.text: (a) Can a comparison sort handle every input of 20 items with at most 61 comparisons? (b) Can a comparison-based algorithm decide whether 2023 distinct items are already sorted using 2022 comparisons? (c) You are given N items with only 3 distinct values. Does the Ω(N log N) bound apply? What’s the best runtime?

hard.answer: (a) No (needs 62) (b) Yes (c) Not as stated; Θ(N) via 3-way partition/counting

solution.text: (a) log₂ 20! ≈ 61.08 (verified), so ≥ 62 comparisons are needed in the worst case.
(b) Checking sortedness is not sorting: compare each adjacent pair, 2022 comparisons, and any unsorted input is detected. The N! argument does not apply because the output is a single yes/no.

(c) The number of distinct outcomes is the number of ways to assign the 3 values, at most 3ᴺ, so the information bound is only log₂ 3ᴺ = Θ(N). One 3-way partition (Dutch national flag) or counting by value sorts in Θ(N).

hard.title: LSD with an unstable digit sort

prompt.text: Someone runs LSD radix sort but uses heapsort (unstable) for each digit pass. Show with a concrete run that the result can be wrong. Would MSD radix sort with heapsort inside each bucket still be correct?

hard.answer: LSD can fail (31, 12, 21, 22 → 12 22 21 31); MSD still works

solution.text: Model an unstable pass by one that reverses ties. Pass 1 (ones digit): ties 31, 21 (digit 1) reversed and 12, 22 (digit 2) reversed → 21 31 22 12. Pass 2 (tens digit): ties 21, 22 (tens 2) reversed → 12 22 21 31. Not sorted (22 before 21). Verified.

MSD with heapsort per bucket: each bucket is sorted (by any correct sort) on its next character and then recursively on the remaining characters, so the relative order of earlier passes is never needed; the result is correct, just not stable.

hard.title: After how many partitions?

prompt.text: Leftmost-pivot Hoare quicksort (recursing on the left part first) is applied to [6, 9, 2, 7, 4, 1, 8, 3]. After how many calls to partition does the array first equal [1 3 2 4 6 7 8 9]? And when is it fully sorted?

hard.answer: After 2 partitions; sorted after the 4th partition

solution.text: Partition 1: [4 3 2 1 6 7 8 9]. Partition 2 (on [4 3 2 1]): [1 3 2 4 6 7 8 9]. Partition 3 (on [1 3 2]): pivot 1 stays. Partition 4 (on [3 2]): [1 2 3 4 6 7 8 9]. Later partitions on [7 8 9] change nothing. Verified.

hard.title: Choose a sort

prompt.text: Pick the best algorithm for each, with a one-line reason: (a) 10⁸ 32-bit ints, minimize time; (b) objects sorted by last name after already being sorted by first name, must keep first-name order on ties; (c) an array where each element is at most 5 positions from its final place; (d) memory limited to O(1) extra, worst case must be O(N log N); (e) 10⁶ strings where most differ in the first 3 characters but some are 10⁵ characters long.

hard.answer: (a) LSD radix (b) mergesort (stable) (c) insertion sort (d) heapsort (e) MSD radix or a comparison sort

solution.text: (a) 4 passes of radix-256 counting sort, Θ(N); or tuned quicksort.
(c) Insertion sort is Θ(N·k) = Θ(N) for k = 5.
(d) Heapsort: in place, Θ(N log N) worst case. (Quicksort’s worst case is Θ(N²); mergesort needs Θ(N) extra.)
(e) MSD radix stops after the distinguishing prefix; LSD would process all 10⁵ characters of the long keys (with padding). A comparison sort also only looks at differing prefixes.

hard.title: Quickselect worst case

prompt.text: Count the partitions and total comparisons (roughly) when leftmost-pivot quickselect searches for the median of the sorted array [1, 2, …, N]. Then explain how a random pivot changes the expected cost.

hard.answer: About N/2 partitions, Θ(N²) comparisons; expected Θ(N) with random pivots

solution.text: Each partition on sorted input puts the pivot at the left end, removing one item. To reach index N/2 takes N/2 partitions of sizes N, N − 1, …, N/2: about (3/8)N² comparisons — Θ(N²). For N = 9: partitions on [0..8], [1..8], [2..8], [3..8], [4..8] (5 partitions) before returning 5 (verified).
Random pivots: expected size shrinks by a constant factor each round, so expected work ≈ N + (3/4)N + (3/4)²N + ⋯ = O(N).

keyFacts: Partition: pivot final, left ≤ pivot ≤ right. Hoare: L stops at ≥ p, G stops at ≤ p, swap, cross → swap pivot with G.
Quicksort Θ(N log N) expected, Θ(N²) worst (sorted input with leftmost pivot); not stable; Θ(log N) stack.
Quickselect: recurse into one side; Θ(N) expected, Θ(N²) worst.
Comparison sorts need ≥ log₂(N!) = Θ(N log N) comparisons (5 items: 7; 20 items: 62).
Counting sort Θ(N + R), stable. LSD radix Θ(W(N + R)), needs a stable per-digit sort.
MSD radix: bucket by first char, recurse per bucket; early exit; doesn’t need stability.
Keys in [0, N²): radix N, 2 passes, Θ(N).

parsons.title: Hoare partition
parsons.goal: Partition a[lo..hi] around the pivot p = a[lo]: L stops at items ≥ p, G stops at items ≤ p, swap misfits, and finally swap the pivot into G’s position. Return the pivot’s final index.
lines: static int partition(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
int p = a[lo], L = lo + 1, G = hi;
while (L <= hi && a[L] < p) L++; while (G > lo && a[G] > p) G--;
distractors: while (L <= hi && a[L] <= p) L++; while (G > lo && a[G] >= p) G--;
